_readme: Snapshot of a real Delta Learning graph, exported by backend/scripts/export_demo_graph.py and loaded by load_demo_graph.py (`make demo`). Embeddings, transcripts and on-screen text are omitted; captured concepts are omitted so the capture beat still has somewhere to go. Segment summaries are model-generated descriptions of third-party talks, included as metadata, not as a reproduction.

videos.title: Game Theory： A Simple Strategy That Will Change Your Life Forever
videos.summary: An animated explainer uses a roommate dishwashing scenario to introduce the Prisoner’s Dilemma and game theory. It explains non-cooperative games, dominant strategies, repeated interactions, and Robert Axelrod’s computer tournament, highlighting the success of Tit-for-Tat.

videos.title: How Decision Making is Actually Science： Game Theory Explained
videos.summary: James Grime introduces game theory through the Prisoner's Dilemma and Nash Equilibrium, then explains cooperative game theory and the Shapley Value using a cookie-baking example to show how joint rewards can be divided fairly.

videos.title: L8_Principal_s_Agentic_Engineering_Workflow
videos.summary: Kun Chen presents an agentic engineering workflow built around terminal tools, memory and skills, automated quality pipelines, long-running agents, parallel worktrees, and a central agent manager that shifts an engineer’s role from implementation toward product leadership.

videos.title: Postgres_is_the_Only_Database_You_Need_in_2026
videos.summary: The video argues that PostgreSQL can replace many components of a typical application stack by providing relational data modeling, JSON document storage, full-text search, job queues, vector similarity search, and graph queries in one ACID-compliant database. It also covers PostgreSQL’s limitations, including sharding, memory usage, and MVCC table bloat.

segments.summary: Kun Chen introduces himself and frames the video as a walkthrough of his agentic engineering workflow, citing experience at major technology companies and large-scale systems.
Kun describes building frontier coding agents and using agents himself to ship dozens of pull requests each day.
Kun explains that he is sharing the workflow freely rather than turning it into a paid course because he wants to focus his business on building products.
Kun previews the workflow’s chapters: core setup followed by recruiting and ramping up agents through memory and skills.
Kun begins his terminal workflow and argues that terminal use keeps hands on the keyboard and provides a consistent environment across platforms.
Kun demonstrates WezTerm, describing its Lua configuration, customization, long history, and cross-platform availability.
Kun introduces tmux and demonstrates panes, tabs, and persistent sessions, allowing agents, editors, and the user to share one terminal workspace.
Kun showcases NeoVim, emphasizing keyboard-centered editing, relative line numbers, navigation, and plugins.
Kun lists four agent harnesses he uses regularly and discusses their differing strengths and constraints.
Kun explains onboarding agents with global and project-level memory files that record preferences and lessons learned from mistakes.
Kun shows how conditionally relevant instructions can be moved out of always-loaded memory files into skills, reducing token consumption.
Kun warns that unvetted third-party skills can introduce security risks and degrade performance, citing a popular skill’s token overhead.
Kun switches to voice input, saying speech is faster than typing and demonstrating OpenSuperWhisper for local transcription.
Kun criticizes GitHub MCP Server for token cost and latency, then promotes Axie principles for designing tools that work more efficiently with agents.
Kun introduces Lavish, which asks agents to create HTML visual prototypes so planning discussions can happen visually rather than through text alone.
Kun demonstrates Lavish’s visual options and comments, explaining that visual feedback makes planning and decisions easier than a terminal text wall.
Kun explains that scaling with agents requires acting more like an engineering manager, trusting automated pipelines instead of manually reviewing every diff.
Kun details the No Mistakes pipeline: branch creation, commits, isolated worktrees, rebasing, adversarial review, end-to-end tests, documentation, and pull request creation.
Kun examines a pull request generated by No Mistakes, including its intent summary, change summary, testing evidence, and risk assessment.
Kun explains that No Mistakes can be triggered directly or as an agent skill, offloading quality-control work and creating more time for planning.
Kun introduces Good Night, Have Fun, a tool that runs long agent loops against an objective until a defined stop condition is reached.
Kun shows Good Night, Have Fun running while he sleeps, with monitoring for token use, iterations, and commits.
Kun explains that long-running loops work best for verifiable objectives such as page-load improvements, end-to-end test coverage, and metric-driven hypothesis experiments.
Kun transitions to parallel agent work and explains that Git worktrees create separate repository directories to prevent agents from conflicting.
Kun introduces Treehouse, a tool he built to create, track, and clean up worktrees automatically.
Kun uses Treehouse to launch three parallel agent sessions to address user feedback from playtesting an AI tutor application.
Kun manages the parallel sessions through tmux tabs and keyboard shortcuts, noting that automated quality pipelines reduce the need for immediate attention.
Kun describes the context-switching burden of managing many agents and introduces FirstMate as a free, open-source central agent manager.
Kun demonstrates FirstMate’s setup process and its role in organizing projects, preferences, and delegated tasks.
Kun asks FirstMate to update three GitHub projects to the latest NPM version, with parallel agents and worktrees handling the work.
Kun asks FirstMate to inspect Lavish Axie’s most recent open issues and identify which are most actionable.
Kun delegates issue 87, concerning annotation mode, to FirstMate while it continues managing other work simultaneously.
Kun reflects that a first mate frees the engineer from execution management and redirects attention to user needs, product direction, and the competitive landscape.
Kun concludes by describing the progression from sailor to captain, promoting his open-source tools, and inviting viewers to subscribe.
The video introduces PostgreSQL as a mature, battle-tested open-source database and argues that it can replace many separate tools in a typical modern technology stack.
A sponsor segment promotes ZTM's project-based engineering courses and a discount code.
The narrator introduces an online-store schema with users, products, and orders connected through foreign keys as a standard relational data model.
A products table uses a JSONB field for flexible product-specific attributes, while GIN indexes make querying those JSON documents fast.
A SQL query filters products by name and additional conditions, returning large and small t-shirt records while showing the related users, products, and orders schema.
PostgreSQL full-text search is presented as a solution for natural-language product searches such as red running shoes, with TS Vector supporting stemming and relevance ranking without Elasticsearch.
A PostgreSQL jobs table functions as a background queue, using SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to avoid duplicate work and LISTEN and NOTIFY to avoid polling.
The PG Vector extension adds native vector storage and similarity search, enabling product recommendations constrained by factors such as visual similarity, inventory, and price.
PostgreSQL 19 native graph queries are used to build a customers-also-bought feature by pattern matching relationships already stored in orders data, without moving data to Neo4j.
The video reviews PostgreSQL as a unified, extensible ACID-compliant system for document storage, search, queues, vectors, and graph queries.

The narrator identifies PostgreSQL's lack of native sharding, per-connection memory overhead, and MVCC table bloat as limitations, while concluding that it remains suitable for most projects below massive scale.
Animated science imagery leads into James Grime introducing game theory as the study of social interactions and its uses in economics, politics, and biology. He identifies John Nash as a key pioneer.

Grime explains that games involve multiple people whose outcomes depend on one another's choices. He distinguishes cooperative from non-cooperative game theory and introduces Wanda and Fred's Prisoner's Dilemma.

A payoff grid shows the Prisoner's Dilemma outcomes. Mutual silence gives Wanda and Fred the best joint outcome, but each has an incentive to confess because silence could lead to a ten-year sentence if the other betrays them.
Grime identifies mutual confession, with five years in jail each, as the Nash Equilibrium. Confession is a dominant strategy because neither player can improve their outcome by changing alone.

Grime turns to cooperative games, in which players pursue a shared goal, such as splitting a restaurant bill or combating climate change. He introduces coalitions and the problem of dividing benefits fairly among contributors.
Grime introduces the Shapley Value for dividing cooperative rewards. He outlines its axioms and begins a cookie-baking example in which two bakers make 40 cookies together but only 30 separately.

The cookie example calculates a Shapley Value allocation. The first baker's marginal contributions are 10 and 20 cookies across possible orders, averaging to 15, so a $40 reward is divided as $15 and $25.

Grime explains that interchangeable players should receive equal shares and dummy players who add nothing should receive nothing. He notes that applying the latter principle may raise ethical concerns in real situations.

The video shows that Shapley Values can be combined across changing parts of a game, such as different workloads or meal costs. For large coalitions, contributions are averaged over every possible order in which players could join.

Grime summarizes that game theory supports strategic behavior in competitive situations and fair reward allocation in cooperative ones, with the Shapley Value handling complex multiplayer contributions.
An animation revisits the cookie-baking example, contrasting batches of 10 and 20 cookies with a joint output of 40 cookies, and connecting the combined production to a $40 reward.
The animation breaks down the shared effort in cookie production, showing how each batch incorporates time spent working on the other baker's output.
Grime concludes that cooperation can produce better outcomes than competition, then promotes SciShow, Patreon supporters, related channels, and social media accounts.
Boot.dev sponsorship and title sequence introduce the video’s Prisoner’s Dilemma theme.
A young adult moves into a two-bedroom apartment and establishes shared chores with a roommate.
The roommates assign weekly dishwashing days, setting up a future choice about whether to fulfill the chore.
After several weeks of mutual compliance, the narrator finds dirty dishes left by the roommate and introduces the strategic conflict.
The roommate scenario is identified as the Prisoner’s Dilemma, where cooperation benefits both parties but each has an incentive to defect.
Game theory is defined as the mathematical study of choices whose outcomes depend on other decision-makers’ actions.
The video describes game theory as a science of strategy applicable from interpersonal interactions to nations.
A rational choice framework is presented: goals and constraints can identify rational choices and optimal strategies, including through simulation.
The narrator states that game theory researchers found an unexpectedly effective strategy across many social and natural conditions.
The video clarifies that a game-theory game is any multi-decision-maker interaction in which each person’s payoff depends on others’ choices.
Game theory is said to encompass conventional games as well as competitive and cooperative interactions between individuals and groups.
Non-cooperative games are introduced as interactions where players independently pursue self-interest, often producing winners and losers.
The British game show Golden Balls is introduced as a Prisoner’s Dilemma-style choice between splitting or stealing money.
The split-or-steal payoff outcomes are explained: mutual splitting shares the money, unilateral stealing takes all, and mutual stealing yields nothing.
A dominant strategy is defined as the action that gives the best result regardless of the other player’s action.
In the one-shot split-or-steal setup, stealing is explained as dominant because it does at least as well against either opposing choice.
The narrator notes that real-life interactions are usually not one-shot games and have continuing consequences.
Business and international actions illustrate how repeated interactions can lead to retaliation, alliances, resource changes, wars, or peace.
Political scientist Robert Axelrod begins a computer-based experiment comparing decision strategies for the Prisoner’s Dilemma.
The tournament format has every submitted program play every other program and itself.
The tournament scoring rules award three points for mutual cooperation, five to a defector against a cooperator, zero to the cooperator, and one each for mutual defection.
Each matchup lasts 200 rounds; fourteen submissions plus a random strategy compete, and total points determine the winner.
The submitted programs include cooperative, early-defecting, exploitative, and randomized strategies such as Grass Camp and Joss.
Repeated tournament runs produce consistent results, with the same strategy—Tit For Tat—emerging as the surprising winner.
The video ends with a brief thank-you and farewell.
